record.field: Create a month's draft payslips for one division — the heart of Payobook.
A four-step wizard that takes one division and one period and computes a draft payslip for every eligible employee.
It is where a month of salaries starts. Everything downstream — review, approval, the bank file — reads what this step produced, so an error here is an error in all of it.
Once the month's attendance and overtime have been imported and committed. Not before: computing on an uncommitted import is the single most common first-week mistake.
The Payroll Officer group, a committed import for the period, and a formula configuration on the division you are running.
Computing before the month's import is committed. The eligible count is the tell — 12 where you expected 48 means the data is not in yet.
Running the wrong cycle. Mid-cycle pays an advance; end-cycle settles the month. They are not two views of one thing.
Submitting for approval without opening the flagged payslips. A flag is a question the engine wants answered, and submitting is you answering it with silence.
Every run on one board, moving draft → Officer → HR → GM → done.
A board of every pay run, grouped by the approval stage it is waiting at, with the actions that stage allows on each card.

Nothing is paid without the right sign-offs, and the board is what makes the pipeline visible and auditable. It answers the only question a payroll week really asks: what is stuck, and whose gate is it stuck at.
Daily during payroll week, and any time you need to know where a period has got to.
A computed run. Approving needs the group that owns that particular gate.
Approving a run without opening its flagged payslips. The board shows totals; the flags are on the slips.
Rejecting without a written reason. The run goes back to draft either way, but the person who has to fix it is then guessing at what you saw.
Reading a status column as a period. The columns are approval stages — July and June can sit in the same one.
Read any employee's slip line by line — gross to net, with every rule visible.
The review surface for individual payslips inside one run: a filterable list, and for the selected employee the approval stepper and the full salary breakdown.
A run total can be right while an individual slip is wrong. This is the only screen that shows the working behind a net figure, so it is where an error is caught before money moves.
After computing and before submitting for approval, and again whenever an employee asks why their pay is what it is.
A computed run to read. No special group is needed to look.
Editing a net amount directly instead of fixing the input and recomputing. The slip then no longer agrees with the data behind it, and the next recompute silently undoes the fix.
Expecting insurance to move when overtime does. BHXH, BHYT and BHTN are charged on the registered base, which overtime does not change.
Clearing a flag by dismissing it. Clearing one means understanding it — the flag was the engine asking a question about that employee.
Bring attendance, overtime and inputs in — preview, score and fix before anything commits.
A guided four-step flow — source, review and match, validate and fix, commit — plus the batch history of everything imported before.
Most wrong payslips start as a wrong row in a file. Fixing it here costs minutes; fixing it after approval costs a retro line and a conversation.
Whenever the month's inputs arrive, and always before computing a run.
The Import group, a file or a connected system to read from, and a formula configuration to map the columns onto.
Committing a batch with unresolved rows because the deadline is close. An unmatched row is an employee who will be missing from the run.
Importing one month's data into another month's period. The batch is named for the period it targets — read that name before committing.
Fixing an import mistake on the payslips afterwards. That corrects the output and leaves the input wrong, so the next recompute brings the mistake back.
Settle a leaver: last salary, unused leave, deductions — one closing statement.
The settlement workspace for departing employees, listing what each is still owed and whether it has been paid.
Leaver settlements have legal deadlines and one chance to be right. They are also the payment most likely to be disputed, because it is the last one.
As soon as a resignation or termination date is confirmed — not on the payroll run date, which is usually too late.
A recorded contract end date and a current leave balance for the employee.
Leaving the departing employee in the normal monthly run as well. They are then paid twice, and recovering an overpayment from someone who has left is a legal problem, not a payroll one.
Settling before the last month's attendance is in. The final salary is a prorated month, so it needs the same inputs every other month needs.
See exactly how a part-month salary was prorated — day by day, no black box.
An audit trail of every prorated amount in a run — joiners, leavers and unpaid leave — showing days worked, standard days and the factor between them.
Proration is the question employees ask most often, and the one hardest to answer from memory. This screen is the evidence, written down before anyone asks.
When a payslip looks too small and you need to show why, and as a spot check on any run with mid-month movement.
A computed run containing at least one joiner, leaver or unpaid-leave case.
Assuming calendar days when the division's configuration uses standard working days. Twenty-two is not thirty, and the difference is somebody's salary.
Reading the money before the factor. If the factor is right and the amount still looks wrong, the problem is upstream in the contract or the import.
Backdated raises and corrections, applied cleanly to a later run — with a full trail.
A ledger of differences owed from periods that are already closed, paid in the current run with the source period recorded on every line.
It keeps closed months closed. Reopening an approved run to fix the past invalidates everything that was reported from it — the retro line is how you pay the difference without doing that.
Backdated raises, allowances missed in an earlier month, and any correction found after the run it belongs to was approved.
The source run is done, and the correction is documented — a retro line without a reason is an unexplained payment.
Editing the old approved payslip instead of creating a retro line. The old month has already been reported; changing it changes a number somebody else has filed.
Leaving the source period blank. Without it the line is money paid for no stated reason, which is exactly what an audit asks about first.
